name: refactor-workflow
applies_when: The correctness claim is that behaviour is unchanged. The work restructures, renames, moves, extracts or consolidates something that already works, the validation that would show it still works already exists, and the job is to carry that validation across rather than to weaken it. Choose this when what you are asking for is judged by whether the system still does exactly what it did before. Work that ends by making a new standing claim -- that something is now the only place a thing happens, that a rule holds from here on -- is not this workflow's work, even where behaviour is unchanged: such a claim needs an assertion nothing asserts today, this workflow has no stage whose work is to write one, and an assertion written under it would be written by the stage whose own change it validates.
max_run_cost_usd_reason: This workflow has no cost corpus of its own yet: no run has executed under it, so there is nothing to derive a figure from. It inherits story-workflow's ceiling until it has one, and story-workflow's reason string carries the derivation. Tighten it against the record runs under this workflow write, not against story-workflow's, since this workflow has one fewer stage and its work is behaviour-preserving rather than new. Nothing reads this key; it records the judgement where a reader of the definition meets the number.

stages.name: implementer
stages.max_execution_cost_usd_reason: This workflow has no cost corpus of its own yet, so it inherits story-workflow's implementer ceiling until it has one; that definition's reason string carries the derivation the figure came from. Nothing reads this key; it records the judgement where a reader of the definition meets the number.
stages.effort_reason: xhigh. The stage that writes the code, and the only stage where raising further costs real money: it carries the largest execution ceiling this definition declares, so the spend here would be paid on every refactor rather than only where judgement is scarcest. Declaring it at all is the other half of the value. Before this key a stage thought as hard as the developer's own editor happened to be set to think, so changing that setting for one unrelated piece of work silently changed how every story was built; a declared level pins it. The spend ordering this rests on is story-workflow's rather than this definition's: it was measured on stories 206, 207 and 208, completed 2026-09-24, each of which ran under story-workflow, and that definition's reason string carries the derivation. This workflow has no cost corpus of its own yet, and its shares will differ in any case, because it declares three stages and no tester where story-workflow declares four. Nothing reads this key; it records the judgement where a reader of the definition meets the value.

stages.name: documenter
stages.max_execution_cost_usd_reason: This workflow has no cost corpus of its own yet, so it inherits story-workflow's documenter ceiling until it has one; that definition's reason string carries the derivation the figure came from. Nothing reads this key; it records the judgement where a reader of the definition meets the number.
stages.effort_reason: high. The narrowest scope of any stage in this workflow -- confined to the configured architecture documents, writing prose and never behaviour, with no test asserting anything about what it produces -- and the smallest execution ceiling this definition declares. Its mistakes are cheap and are corrected by a correction pass rather than by a retry, so it is the one stage here that is not bought up. The share story-workflow's reason cites for its own documenter was measured on runs of that definition, which declares a tester stage this one does not, so it is not this definition's share, and this workflow has no cost corpus of its own yet to put in its place. Nothing reads this key; it records the judgement where a reader of the definition meets the value.

stages.name: verifier
stages.max_execution_cost_usd_reason: This workflow has no cost corpus of its own yet, so it inherits story-workflow's verifier ceiling until it has one; that definition's reason string carries the derivation the figure came from. Nothing reads this key; it records the judgement where a reader of the definition meets the number.
stages.effort_reason: max. The gate the whole run passes through, and its misjudgements are the expensive kind: a verdict that passes broken work ships it, and a verdict that fails sound work spends a retry on nothing. It is also the cheapest place in the system to buy better judgement: taking one stage of three from the default to the ceiling costs a fraction of what one avoided retry costs. It matters more here than under story-workflow, because this definition declares no tester stage: its entire claim that behaviour is unchanged rests on the suite census and on this one judgement, so there is no second reading of the work to catch what this stage misses. That same absence is why the share story-workflow's reason cites for its own verifier is not this definition's -- it was measured on runs that included the tester this one does not declare -- and this workflow has no cost corpus of its own yet to put in its place. Nothing reads this key; it records the judgement where a reader of the definition meets the value.

inspection.effort_reason: xhigh. The pre-stage inspection is a large judgement spend of its own, and what it writes is read by a person as well as by the stage that judges the story -- so both a miss and a false alarm cost something, the miss silently and the false alarm in the reading. It stops one level short of the ceiling because it is a large spend and because it supplies rather than decides: nothing it reports can fail a run. It is declared here rather than on the stage because the inspection is a separate invocation the stage does not make, so the level the stage itself runs at says nothing about it. The ranking story-workflow's reason gives the same invocation was measured on runs of that definition, which declares a stage this one does not, so it does not carry across; this workflow has no cost corpus of its own yet to rank against. Nothing reads this key; it records the judgement where a reader of the definition meets the value.
inspection.result_reason: The run-directory artifact the pre-stage inspection writes for this stage to read: the Inspector's findings about the files this refactor itself changed. Shaped like the clean_clone and correction_pass declarations beside it -- the key's absence disables the mechanism for the workflow with no code change, and the artifact name lives here rather than in orchestration. A refactor answers its own review for the reason a story does: a review comment on a change belongs to the change that produced it, and only a finding about a file the change did not touch is a backlog item. It is evidence and not a verdict: no coordinator branch reads it, and the verifier's existing triage decides what it is worth.

repair_pass.budget_reason: Two rather than one, on the correction pass's arithmetic: a pass fixes the findings a verification raises, and the verification after it can find one the first findings did not reach, and a separate story to carry a leftover finding costs more than a second pass in the run that found it. Bounded at all because a repair pass may change behaviour, which is why it carries the findings and no guidance, routes only after the clean-clone check on the routing verdict has passed, and returns to a verification that runs the check again on the repaired tree. The stage comes off the retry_routing table below rather than off this declaration, so a finding is fixed by the stage that owns its file. Nothing reads this key; it records the judgement where a reader of the definition meets the budget.

implementation.when: the defect is in the change itself: behaviour the refactor was meant to preserve is not preserved, the restructuring the story asked for is missing or incomplete, or an edit to the existing validation weakened what it checks rather than carrying it across

documentation.when: the defect is in the documentation itself: it describes behaviour the code does not have, names a file, module or symbol that does not exist, contradicts what the run's own artifacts record, or omits a change the story required be written down. Judge the document against the code as it now stands: a document that accurately describes wrong behaviour is an implementation defect, not a documentation one, and belongs to the category that owns the code
